Krakow Military Section on Municipal Cemetery

Jewish Cemetery · Kraków, Poland

Not demolished. Jews are first recorded in Kraków in the 12th century; settlement developed in Kazimierz from the late 15th century (incorporated into the city in 1800). Famed Rabbi Mosze Isserles (the Remu), author of Ha-Mapah, lived in Kraków; most of the city's Jews were murdered in the Holocaust, though over a dozen Jewish organizations remain active today. This military section, established around 1915 by the Austro-Hungarian military's War Cemeteries Department as a burial site for Jewish soldiers killed in WWI, was designed by Hans Mayr with an ambitious mausoleum plan - never fully realized - featuring lion sculptures and a menorah. As built, it held 161 single and 14 collective graves (175 total), nearly all Austro-Hungarian soldiers with 3 likely from the Russian Army; each stone bore bilingual Polish-Hebrew inscriptions beneath a Star of David. Postwar burials added veterans Markus Dąbek (d. 1919), Juda Filozof (d. 1920), and Dawid Beer (d. 1921, a war-invalid hospital patient). Extensive damage has reduced the site to 26 surviving tombstones, several relocated to the entrance wall after 1945.
